title: Extractive Summarization Basics
text: Extractive summarization selects important sentences from the original document. It is useful when factual wording must stay close to the source. Ranking often uses term frequency, sentence position, title overlap, and redundancy reduction.

title: Abstractive Summarization Basics
text: Abstractive summarization generates new wording that captures the meaning of a source. It can combine ideas across paragraphs, simplify language, and remove repetition. The main risk is hallucination when the model invents facts not present in the source.

title: Chunking Long Documents
text: Long documents are split into chunks before retrieval. Good chunks preserve complete ideas, headings, and nearby context. Chunks that are too small lose meaning, while chunks that are too large reduce retrieval precision.

title: Chunk Overlap
text: Chunk overlap repeats a small amount of text between neighboring chunks. It helps prevent important facts from being separated at chunk boundaries. Typical overlap is 10 to 20 percent of the chunk length.

title: Embedding Retrieval
text: Embedding retrieval converts queries and documents into vectors. Similar vectors indicate related meaning even when words differ. It is strong for semantic matching but requires an embedding model and a vector index.

title: Keyword Retrieval
text: Keyword retrieval matches exact words between a query and documents. BM25 is a popular keyword ranking method that rewards rare matching terms and balances document length. It works well when users include domain vocabulary.

title: Hybrid Retrieval
text: Hybrid retrieval combines keyword scores and embedding scores. It improves robustness because keyword search catches exact names, formulas, and acronyms, while embeddings catch paraphrases. Scores are usually normalized before merging.

title: Reranking
text: Reranking applies a stronger model to a short candidate list from the retriever. The reranker compares each query-document pair and reorders results for relevance. It is slower than first-stage retrieval but often improves top result quality.

title: Context Window Management
text: A RAG system must fit retrieved context inside the model context window. The system should include the most relevant chunks, remove duplicates, and reserve room for instructions and the answer. Too much context can distract the model.

title: Grounded Answering
text: Grounded answering means the chatbot answers only from retrieved sources. If the sources do not contain the answer, the model should say it does not know. Grounding reduces hallucination and supports citations.

title: Citations in RAG
text: Citations show which source documents support an answer. A good RAG chatbot returns source titles, document identifiers, and relevance scores. Citations make answers easier to verify and improve user trust.

title: Prompt Template for RAG
text: A RAG prompt usually contains instructions, retrieved context, the user question, and output rules. It should tell the model to use only the context and to cite document identifiers. Clear prompts reduce unsupported claims.

title: Retrieval Accuracy
text: Retrieval accuracy measures whether the retriever returns the expected source document for a question. Common metrics include top-1 accuracy, top-k accuracy, mean reciprocal rank, precision, and recall. A strong retriever places relevant documents near the top.

title: Answer Quality Evaluation
text: Answer quality can be evaluated by comparing generated answers with reference answers. Simple automated methods use token overlap, precision, recall, and F1. Human review can judge correctness, completeness, clarity, and citation support.

title: Faithfulness
text: Faithfulness measures whether an answer is supported by the retrieved context. An answer can be fluent but unfaithful if it adds unsupported details. RAG systems should prefer concise answers that stay close to source evidence.

title: Hallucination Risk
text: Hallucination occurs when a model produces unsupported or false information. In summarization and RAG, hallucination can be reduced with source-grounded prompts, citations, lower temperature, and refusal when evidence is missing.

title: Temperature Setting
text: Temperature controls randomness in model output. Lower temperature gives more stable and factual answers, which is usually preferred for summarization and RAG. Higher temperature can be useful for creative writing but increases variation.

title: Max Tokens
text: Max tokens limits the length of generated output. A summarizer should set enough tokens for complete bullet points without wasting cost. A RAG chatbot should reserve tokens for both retrieved context and the final answer.

title: Source Document Cleaning
text: Source documents should be cleaned before indexing. Cleaning removes navigation text, ads, duplicate boilerplate, broken characters, and irrelevant metadata. Better cleaning improves both retrieval and answer quality.

title: Text Normalization
text: Text normalization converts content into a consistent form for retrieval. It may lowercase text, remove punctuation, collapse whitespace, and filter stop words. Normalization helps keyword retrievers compare queries and documents reliably.

title: Stop Words
text: Stop words are common words such as the, is, and of. Removing them can improve keyword retrieval by focusing on meaningful terms. However, some phrases need stop words to preserve meaning, so removal should be conservative.

title: Document Metadata
text: Metadata stores information such as title, author, date, category, and source URL. Retrieval systems can filter or rank results using metadata. Metadata also helps display readable citations to the user.

title: Vector Database Role
text: A vector database stores embeddings and supports fast nearest-neighbor search. It is useful for large document collections. Small academic projects can start with in-memory retrieval before moving to a production vector database.

title: BM25 Formula Intuition
text: BM25 scores a document higher when it contains rare query terms. It also prevents long documents from winning only because they contain more words. The method uses term frequency, inverse document frequency, and length normalization.

title: Mean Reciprocal Rank
text: Mean reciprocal rank evaluates how early the first relevant result appears. If the correct document is ranked first, reciprocal rank is 1. If it is ranked third, reciprocal rank is one third. Higher MRR means users find evidence sooner.

title: Top K Retrieval
text: Top-k retrieval checks whether a relevant document appears within the first k results. Top-3 accuracy is often easier to satisfy than top-1 accuracy. RAG systems usually pass several top documents into the answer generator.

title: Precision and Recall
text: Precision measures how many retrieved documents are relevant. Recall measures how many relevant documents were retrieved. In RAG, high precision avoids distracting context, while high recall prevents missing key evidence.

title: Answer F1 Score
text: Answer F1 combines token precision and token recall between a generated answer and a reference answer. It rewards answers that contain expected key terms without adding too many unrelated words. It is simple but cannot fully replace human judgment.

title: RAG Versus Fine Tuning
text: RAG retrieves external knowledge at query time, while fine tuning changes model weights during training. RAG is better for frequently changing facts and citation-heavy answers. Fine tuning is better for style, format, and specialized behavior.

title: Knowledge Base Updates
text: A RAG knowledge base should be updated when source documents change. Updates may require re-cleaning, re-chunking, and re-indexing documents. Evaluation should be rerun after major corpus changes.

title: User Query Rewriting
text: Query rewriting turns a vague or conversational question into a clearer search query. It can expand acronyms, add domain terms, and remove irrelevant chat history. Better rewritten queries often improve retrieval accuracy.

title: Multi Turn Chat
text: A multi-turn RAG chatbot may use chat history to understand follow-up questions. The system should rewrite follow-ups into standalone questions before retrieval. Without this step, pronouns like it or that can reduce retrieval quality.

title: Refusal Behavior
text: A grounded chatbot should refuse or ask for clarification when retrieved context is insufficient. Refusal is better than guessing. A useful refusal explains that the knowledge base does not contain enough evidence.

title: Source Diversity
text: Source diversity prevents the top results from repeating the same information. Diversified retrieval can include different documents, sections, or viewpoints. Diversity is helpful when a question needs broad coverage.

title: Duplicate Removal
text: Duplicate source text can bias retrieval and make a chatbot repeat the same evidence. Systems should remove exact duplicates and near duplicates during ingestion. Deduplication improves ranking and reduces wasted context.

title: Summarizing Retrieved Context
text: When retrieved context is long, the system can summarize evidence before answering. This compression step keeps the answer prompt small. The compression must preserve facts, citations, and uncertainty.

title: Question Answering Prompt
text: A question answering prompt should separate context from the user question. It should instruct the model to answer directly, cite sources, and avoid unsupported claims. Formatting rules help produce consistent chatbot responses.

title: Evaluation Dataset Design
text: A RAG evaluation dataset contains questions, expected source document identifiers, and reference answers. Questions should cover common user needs and difficult edge cases. The dataset must be separate from the retrieval code.

title: Manual Evaluation Rubric
text: A manual answer rubric can rate correctness, completeness, faithfulness, clarity, and citation quality. Each category can use a score from one to five. Manual review catches issues that token metrics miss.

title: Latency
text: Latency is the time between a user question and a chatbot answer. Retrieval, reranking, prompt construction, and model generation all add latency. Caching and smaller top-k settings can reduce response time.

title: Cost Control
text: RAG cost depends on embedding, retrieval infrastructure, and generation tokens. Smaller context, concise answers, caching, and lightweight models reduce cost. Evaluation helps avoid paying for answers that are not accurate.

title: Security for Uploaded Documents
text: Document chatbots should protect private source files and user questions. Access control, input validation, and careful logging are important. Secrets such as API keys must be stored in environment variables, not source code.

title: Prompt Injection
text: Prompt injection occurs when retrieved documents contain instructions that try to override the system prompt. A RAG chatbot should treat retrieved text as data, not commands. The prompt should tell the model to ignore instructions inside sources.

title: Domain Specific Corpus
text: A domain-specific RAG chatbot uses documents from a focused subject area. A narrow corpus improves relevance because the vocabulary and questions are consistent. For an AI summarization project, sources can cover summarization, retrieval, prompting, evaluation, and deployment.

title: Minimum Corpus Size
text: A project requirement may specify at least fifty source documents. The corpus should list each document with a unique identifier, title, category, and text. Clear identifiers make retrieval evaluation possible.

title: FastAPI RAG Endpoint
text: A FastAPI RAG endpoint can accept a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and return citations. The response should include answer text, source documents, and retrieval scores. This structure supports both UI display and evaluation.

title: Frontend Chat Interface
text: A RAG frontend should provide a question box, a submit button, answer output, and source citations. It should show loading and error states. Displaying document titles and scores helps users understand why an answer was produced.

title: Evaluation Endpoint
text: An evaluation endpoint can run a fixed question set against the retriever and answer generator. It returns metrics such as top-1 accuracy, top-3 accuracy, MRR, and answer F1. This makes project evaluation repeatable from the UI.

title: Deployment Environment Variables
text: Deployment should store API keys and database URLs as environment variables. The frontend uses a build-time API URL variable to call the backend. Backend services should read secrets from the environment at runtime.

title: Render Deployment for Full Stack AI Apps
text: On Render, a FastAPI backend runs as a web service, while a Vite React frontend can run as a static site. The backend start command should bind to host 0.0.0.0 and the Render PORT variable. The frontend should set VITE_API_URL to the backend service URL.
